result: Undifferentiated hESCs express only six TAFs (TAFs 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, and 11), while seven TAFs (TAFs 1, 4, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13) are undetectable. This pattern was confirmed by immunoblot, qRT-PCR, and observed in both H9 and H1 hESC lines.
evaluation: Claims C1, C29, C30 are directly supported by immunoblot (Figure 1A), qRT-PCR (Figure 1B), and replicated in H1 cells (C32, Figure 1—figure supplement 3). The antibody specificity was validated by RNAi knockdown (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2). Multiple orthogonal methods converge on the same conclusion.

result: Following retinoic acid-induced differentiation, the seven TAFs absent in undifferentiated hESCs (TAFs 1, 4, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13) are induced, while the six hESC TAFs remain at relatively constant levels. This is accompanied by loss of OCT4 and induction of differentiation markers.
evaluation: Claims C2, C37, C38 are supported by immunoblot analysis (Figure 1D) showing TAF induction upon differentiation. The differentiation is validated by OCT4 loss and NES induction (C35, C36). This provides strong evidence that TAF composition changes during differentiation.

result: hESCs contain a non-canonical TBP-containing complex comprising TAFs 2, 6, 7, 11, and TBP, but not TAFs 3 and 5. TAFs 2, 6, 7, 11 co-sediment at ~440 kDa with TBP, while TAFs 3 and 5 fractionate heterogeneously with substantial free protein.
evaluation: Claims C39-C45 are supported by sucrose gradient sedimentation (Figure 2A) and co-immunoprecipitation (Figure 2B). The biochemical evidence consistently shows TAFs 2, 6, 7, 11 form a stable complex with TBP, while TAFs 3 and 5 do not co-immunoprecipitate with TBP. The molecular weight estimate (~440 kDa) is consistent with the proposed composition.

result: Most active genes in hESCs (class I genes) are bound by only TAFs 3 and 5 along with TBP. ChIP-chip analysis shows the vast majority of active genes have promoter-bound TAF3 and TAF5, with validation rates of 92.3% for TAF3 and 100% for TAF5.
evaluation: Claims C3, C48, C58 are supported by directed ChIP (Figure 3B) and genome-wide ChIP-chip (Figure 6A). The high validation rates (C66, C67) from directed ChIP experiments (Figure 7B) confirm the ChIP-chip predictions. The convergence of multiple experimental approaches strongly supports this result.

result: A smaller fraction of active genes (class II genes) are bound by all six hESC TAFs (TAFs 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 11) along with TBP. TAF7 and TAF11 show substantial overlap (92.3% co-occupancy), and genes bound by TAF7/11 are also bound by TAF2 and TAF6.
evaluation: Claims C4, C49, C59-C61 are supported by ChIP (Figure 3B) and ChIP-chip (Figure 6B, 6C). The high validation rates for TAF7 (88.9%, C64) and TAF11 (96.4%, C65) and their co-occupancy (92.3%, C70) are confirmed by directed ChIP (Figure 7B). TAF2 and TAF6 co-occupancy at TAF7/11 sites (C71, Figure 7C) further validates the complex composition.

result: The same transcriptionally active genes use different TAF complexes in different cell types. Seven class I genes show TAF3 and TAF5 recruitment in both HeLa and H9 cells, but TAFs 2, 6, 7, 11 are only recruited in HeLa cells, demonstrating remarkable plasticity of the transcription machinery.
evaluation: Claims C51-C53 are supported by comparative ChIP analysis (Figure 4C) showing differential TAF occupancy on the same genes in HeLa vs H9 cells. This demonstrates that housekeeping genes can be activated by diverse core promoter complexes, supporting the plasticity claim (C110). The experimental design directly tests the hypothesis.

result: TAF occupancy correlates with transcriptional activity in hESCs. Knockdown of TAFs 3 and 5 reduces expression of both class I and II genes, while knockdown of TAFs 2, 6, 7, 11 only affects class II genes, establishing a strong relationship between TAF occupancy and gene expression.
evaluation: Claims C54-C56 are supported by qRT-PCR analysis following siRNA-mediated knockdown (Figure 5A, 5B). The differential effects on class I vs class II genes match the predicted occupancy patterns. Results were replicated with independent siRNAs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), strengthening the conclusion.

result: Depleting hESC TAFs induces differentiation and loss of pluripotency. shRNA-mediated knockdown of each of the six hESC TAFs decreases alkaline phosphatase-positive colonies, induces differentiation markers (AFP, CGB7, IGF2, NES, SOX1), and decreases pluripotency gene expression (NANOG, OCT4).
evaluation: Claims C6, C72-C76 are supported by multiple assays: alkaline phosphatase staining (Figure 8A), qRT-PCR for differentiation markers (Figure 8B), and pluripotency genes (Figure 8C, Figure 5). Results were replicated with independent shRNAs/siRNAs (Figure 8—figure supplements 2-4). The convergence of multiple differentiation markers strongly supports the conclusion.

result: Ectopic expression of TAFs absent from hESCs induces differentiation and selectively affects class II genes. TAF1 overexpression decreases alkaline phosphatase-positive colonies, induces differentiation markers, decreases NANOG and OCT4 expression, and prevents TBP/POL2 recruitment to the OCT4 promoter. Class I genes are unaffected or modestly increased.
evaluation: Claims C7, C77-C84, C117 are supported by alkaline phosphatase staining (Figure 8E), qRT-PCR (Figure 8F, 8G), immunoblot (Figure 8H), and ChIP (Figure 8I). The selective effect on class II genes (C80, C81) matches the predicted TAF occupancy patterns. Multiple TAFs show similar effects (C82), while endogenous TAFs do not (C83), providing important controls.

result: The selective expression and use of TAFs underlies hESC self-renewal. Altering TAF composition by either depletion or ectopic expression results in misregulated gene expression and differentiation, demonstrating that the unusual TAF composition is required for hESCs to maintain pluripotency and self-renew.
evaluation: Claims C8, C85, C113 are inferred conclusions supported by the combined evidence from knockdown (C6, C72-C76) and overexpression (C7, C77-C84) experiments. Both gain- and loss-of-function approaches converge on the same conclusion. However, this is a correlative conclusion; causality is inferred but not definitively proven through rescue experiments.

result: Class I gene promoters have greater H3K4me3 than class II gene promoters. This difference is statistically significant (p<1.2e-13) and may relate to TAF3's PHD finger domain that can bind H3K4me3.
evaluation: Claims C62, C105 are supported by ChIP-chip analysis (Figure 6E) and statistical analysis (Table 1, p<1.2e-13). The connection to TAF3's PHD domain (C104) is supported by citation. However, the functional significance of this difference is not experimentally tested in this study.

result: Class II genes have significantly more alternative promoters than class I genes (p<1.7e-58). The average number of alternative promoters is 0.934 for class II genes vs 0.686 for class I genes.
evaluation: Claim C63 is supported by ChIP-chip analysis (Figure 6F) and statistical analysis (Table 1, p<1.7e-58). The difference is highly significant. However, the functional significance of this association is not explored experimentally.

result: TAF6 is expressed in both HeLa and H9 cells, but different isoforms predominate: the short delta form in H9 cells and the larger alpha/beta form in HeLa cells.
evaluation: Claim C31 is supported by immunoblot analysis (Figure 1A) showing different molecular weight bands for TAF6 in the two cell types. The isoform identification is based on molecular weight, which is a standard approach.

result: All other general transcription factors (GTFs) analyzed besides TAFs were comparably expressed in HeLa and H9 cells, including TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIIE, TFIIF, TFIIH, TBP, POL2, and mediator subunits.
evaluation: Claim C34 is supported by immunoblot analysis (Figure 1C). This is an important control showing that the TAF differences are specific and not part of a general transcription machinery difference.

result: The TAF composition of hESCs is unprecedented and likely unique to hESCs. Mouse ESCs express all TFIID TAFs analyzed, unlike hESCs, demonstrating species-specific differences in TAF expression.
evaluation: Claims C86, C87 are supported by immunoblot analysis of mouse ESCs (Figure 9) and comparison with prior literature. The claim of uniqueness (C86) is somewhat speculative but supported by the comparison with mouse ESCs and cited reviews showing no similar pattern in other cell types.

result: A model is proposed where a stable TBP/TAF 2,6,7,11 complex is recruited to class II genes, while TAFs 3 and 5 are recruited independently to all active genes.
evaluation: Claims C89, C90 are inferred from the biochemical (Figure 2) and ChIP (Figures 3-7) data. The model is consistent with all observations: TAFs 2,6,7,11 form a stable complex with TBP but not with TAFs 3,5; TAFs 3,5 are found at all active genes while TAFs 2,6,7,11 are only at class II genes. However, this is a model based on inference rather than direct demonstration.

result: hESCs contain only three HFD-containing TAFs (3, 6, 11) which cannot form any of the five known TAF heterodimers (TAF3–10, TAF6–9, TAF4–12, TAF8–10, TAF11–13), suggesting major differences in assembly and structure between TFIID and the hESC TBP/TAF complex.
evaluation: Claims C100, C101 are logical inferences based on established knowledge about TAF heterodimers (C97, C98, C99) and the observed TAF expression pattern (C1). The reasoning is sound: if the HFD-containing TAFs present cannot form known heterodimers important for TFIID assembly, the hESC complex must assemble differently. However, this is an inference rather than direct experimental demonstration.

result: Gene ontology analysis did not reveal any functional category differentially enriched in class I or class II genes.
evaluation: Claim C106 is stated as a negative result from gene ontology analysis. While the data are not shown, this is a straightforward analysis and the negative result is clearly stated.

result: Pluripotency factors are found in both gene classes: OCT4 and NANOG are class II genes, while SOX2, DPPA4, and KLF4 are class I genes.
evaluation: Claims C107, C108 are supported by ChIP analysis (Figure 3B, Figure 10). This demonstrates that gene function (pluripotency) does not predict TAF class, which is an important observation for understanding the biological significance of the two classes.

result: A developmental model is proposed where undifferentiated hESCs start with specialized transcription machinery (incomplete TFIID), switch to complete TFIID during differentiation, then specialize again in some terminal differentiation programs.
evaluation: Claim C122 integrates the current findings (C1, C2) with prior literature (C19, C20, C119, C120, C121). The model is logical and consistent with all available data. However, it is based on inference across different studies and cell types rather than direct longitudinal tracking in a single system.

result: Approximately 3600 high-confidence actively transcribed genes were defined based on co-occupancy of TBP and POL2 at transcription start sites.
evaluation: Claim C57 is supported by ChIP-chip analysis (Figure 6—figure supplements 1–3). This is a methodological result defining the gene set for subsequent analyses. The approach of using TBP+POL2 co-occupancy to define active genes is standard.

result: The authors speculate that transcriptional induction of TAFs absent from undifferentiated hESCs may be part of the mechanism by which pluripotency genes are silenced during differentiation.
evaluation: Claim C118 is explicitly speculative. While supported by the observation that ectopic TAF expression silences pluripotency genes (C117), this is a hypothesis about the normal differentiation process that has not been directly tested. The speculation is reasonable but requires experimental validation.

result: The authors suggest that altering the composition of basic transcription machinery, particularly TAFs, may be a powerful mechanism for developmental reprogramming.
evaluation: Claim C123 is speculative, extrapolating from the current findings to broader developmental biology. While the data support that TAF composition changes are important for hESC differentiation, the claim about developmental reprogramming more broadly is not directly tested.
